title: Add gradient clipping to the dnn training loop
description:
There is no gradient clipping anywhere in wirecell/dnn/train.py. Adding it is the
standard remedy for the divergence recorded in wcpy-pqx, and it targets the cause (an outsized
update to the attention branch) rather than the symptom (gates collapsing in response).

EVIDENCE. In the stage-1 run in wcpy-pqx the attention block weight norms grew smoothly at
about +2 per epoch for six epochs, then jumped 6-9x that in one epoch:

  block norms   epoch 0 [14.04, 15.23] ... epoch 5 [22.87, 25.38] -> epoch 6 [35.93, 36.32]

i.e. +57% and +43% in a single epoch against a trend of roughly +13%/epoch. Simultaneously the
head norms fell 21-35% and the gammas collapsed. Clipping bounds exactly the kind of update
that produced that jump.

Note the norms were on a monotonic ramp from epoch 0 with no sign of levelling, and AdamW's
default weight_decay=0.01 (see apps/xvunet/__init__.py:24) was not holding them. So this is not
purely a one-off spike; the run was trending toward instability the whole time.

IMPLEMENTATION
- torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(parameters, max_norm) in Classifier.epoch (train.py), after
  backward and before optimizer.step().
- Under AMP the gradients must be unscaled first, or the clip threshold is applied to scaled
  values and means nothing. With torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler that is scaler.unscale_(optimizer)
  before the clip. Note this codebase only enables GradScaler for fp16, and xvunet requires
  bfloat16 which needs no scaler -- so the unscale path matters for the other apps, not xvunet.
  Get it right for both.
- Under DDP, clip after backward so gradients are already all-reduced. Clipping per-rank before
  synchronisation would apply a different effective threshold depending on world size.
- Make it opt-in and configurable, e.g. a [train] grad_clip key, default None/off so existing
  runs are unchanged.
- Log when clipping actually fires, or at least the observed grad norm, so 'clipping is on' is
  distinguishable from 'clipping is doing something'. clip_grad_norm_ returns the pre-clip
  total norm, which is worth recording per epoch alongside the gamma magnitudes.

BENEFITS EVERY APP, not just xvunet -- it lives in the shared Classifier.

RELATED: wcpy-pqx (the divergence this addresses), wcpy-jrn (lr scheduling, the other half of
the stability story). Clipping and a lower lr compose; do both rather than choosing.
acceptance_criteria: grad_clip is configurable from [train] and defaults to off; clipping happens after backward and, under AMP with a scaler, after unscale_; observed pre-clip grad norm recorded per epoch; the wcpy-pqx configuration reruns past epoch 6 without gate collapse with clipping enabled

title: xvunet: LayerScale gates collapse mid-training at lr=4e-3, loss reverts toward trunk baseline
description:
OBSERVED. Stage-1 run (frozen trunks, attn_mode=all, adamw, learning_rate=0.004,
b=4 per rank under DDP, n=15880 train / 3970 eval) trained normally for six epochs then
destabilised. The gates collapsed and the loss reverted most of the way to the trunk baseline.

Output gammas, one per view:

  epoch 0  [ 0.1905,  0.1585, -0.2005]
  epoch 1  [ 0.2472,  0.2082, -0.2764]
  epoch 2  [ 0.2701,  0.2402, -0.3164]
  epoch 3  [ 0.2845,  0.2561, -0.3437]
  epoch 4  [ 0.2856,  0.2665, -0.3582]
  epoch 5  [ 0.2895,  0.2737, -0.3721]     <- smooth monotonic opening to here
  epoch 6  [ 0.0476, -0.0885, -0.1172]     <- collapse; V crosses zero
  epoch 7  [ 0.0908, -0.1089, -0.1128]

Losses:
  epoch 5  train 2.6220e-03  eval 2.5722e-03    (best)
  epoch 6  train 4.1877e-03  eval 3.4665e-03
  epoch 7  train 3.4672e-03  eval 3.3890e-03

Magnitudes at epoch 6: U down 84%, W down 69%, V flips sign. Since gamma scales the entire
cross-view correction, collapsing it reverts the model toward the pure-trunk output, which is
consistent with eval landing near the frozen-trunk baseline.

LIKELY MECHANISM. Adam's step is bounded by about lr per step, so moving gamma by 0.25 needs
roughly 60 sustained steps out of 3970 in an epoch -- not one catastrophic step. Gradient
descent driving gamma down while loss rises does not make sense on its own, so the more
coherent reading is that the BRANCH WEIGHTS diverged first (qkv, proj, fuses, heads), making
the correction actively harmful, and gamma was then pulled toward zero as damage control. The
gate collapse is the symptom; the branch blow-up is the cause. CHECK: compare
||blocks.*.qkv.weight|| and ||heads.*.weight|| between the epoch-5 and epoch-6 checkpoints.

WHY THE LR IS THE SUSPECT. While gamma is near zero the gradient reaching the branch weights
is proportional to gamma, so early training is intrinsically stable. As the gates open that
gradient grows, so a learning rate that is safe at gamma=0 can be unstable at gamma=0.3. This
model therefore gets RISKIER as it trains, which is the opposite of the usual assumption.
learning_rate=0.004 is 2x the 2e-3 threshold the optimizer warns about for Adam-family rates;
the warning is silent here only because name=adamw is set explicitly, which is that guard
working as designed. The documented stage-1 value in the project notes is 1e-3.

DO NOT WAIT FOR RECOVERY. By epoch 7 train had recovered 46% of its excess over the epoch-5
best but eval only 8.7%, and V's gamma continued further negative while U re-opened. The model
is rebuilding in a different configuration rather than retracing, so there is no reason to
expect it to rejoin the epoch-5 trajectory.

REMEDY: restart from the epoch-5 checkpoint at learning_rate=1e-3. Longer term see wcpy-jrn --
a decaying schedule would lower the rate before the danger zone, and the zero-init gating
gives that an unusually concrete justification since the effective gradient scale genuinely
changes during training.

MONITORING: gamma norms are not currently recorded per epoch. epoch_history holds losses only,
so this collapse was only detectable by pulling checkpoints apart after the fact. Recording
per-epoch gamma magnitudes would make it visible live and costs nothing.

CONFIRMED (follow-up): weight norms across the collapse settle cause vs symptom. The branch
diverged FIRST; the gates and heads were suppressed in response.

  attention block weight norms (2 blocks)
    epoch 0 [14.035, 15.231]
    epoch 1 [16.170, 17.346]
    epoch 2 [17.972, 19.410]
    epoch 3 [19.744, 21.476]
    epoch 4 [21.380, 23.420]
    epoch 5 [22.873, 25.385]
    epoch 6 [35.927, 36.316]   <- +57% and +43% in one epoch
    epoch 7 [34.715, 34.946]

  head weight norms (3 heads, one per view)
    epoch 0 [1.489, 1.433, 1.558]
    epoch 5 [1.733, 1.504, 1.752]
    epoch 6 [1.362, 1.070, 1.135]   <- down 21%, 29%, 35%
    epoch 7 [1.373, 1.028, 1.091]

So at epoch 6 the block norms jumped 6-9x their usual per-epoch increment while the heads AND
the gammas both shrank. The model suppressed the now-harmful correction through two channels at
once. This confirms the 'likely mechanism' above and closes the CHECK it asked for.

TWO FURTHER OBSERVATIONS

1. The block norms were on a monotonic ramp from epoch 0 (14.0 -> 22.9 and 15.2 -> 25.4, about
   +13%/epoch) with no sign of levelling off. The collapse was the endpoint of a visible trend,
   not a random spike. AdamW's default weight_decay=0.01 was not holding them. A norm ramp like
   this is itself an early-warning signal worth monitoring.

2. The post-collapse state is pathological, not merely worse: at epoch 7 the block norms are
   still ~40% above epoch 5 while the gammas and heads stay suppressed. Large branch weights
   throttled by small gates is a poor configuration to climb out of, which reinforces
   restarting from the epoch-5 checkpoint over waiting for recovery.

REMEDY LIST, cheapest first:
  a) lower learning_rate to 1e-3 (campaign configs currently ship 4e-3)
  b) add gradient clipping -- see wcpy-04x. There is none in train.py today. This targets the
     cause rather than the symptom and helps every app.
  c) optionally raise weight_decay on the branch parameters.
These compose; do (a) and (b) rather than choosing between them.
acceptance_criteria: Gate collapse reproduced or ruled out at lr=1e-3 with a run long enough to clear the epoch-6 danger zone; branch weight norms compared across the epoch 5/6 boundary to confirm cause vs symptom; per-epoch gamma magnitudes recorded in epoch_history; the failure mode and its lr dependence documented in the xvunet module docstring; campaign configs updated off 4e-3

title: Implement gdml_transform and world-frame transform chain (numpy/scipy)
description: Implement the coordinate transform utilities in wirecell/util/gdml.py based on the research in wcpy-8o7. Required functions: (1) gdml_transform(pos_xyz_mm, rot_xyz_deg) -> 4x4 ndarray: builds a local-to-world homogeneous matrix from a GDML physvol position and rotation. Uses scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation.from_euler('xyz', angles, degrees=True).inv() for the active rotation. (2) compose_transforms(*transforms) -> 4x4 ndarray: multiplies a sequence of 4x4 matrices parent-first. (3) apply_transform(T, point_local) -> point_world: applies a 4x4 homogeneous matrix to a 3-vector. Write tests FIRST (red/green): test_identity_transform (pos=0, rot=0 leaves point unchanged), test_pure_translation, test_single_axis_rotation (x=90 deg rotates Z->Y as expected), test_rUWireAboutX_direction (x=150 gives wire at 30 deg from Z), test_two_level_composition (translation then rotation). NOTE: GDML tube z attribute is FULL length; half_L = z/2. Tests should cover this.
close_reason: Implemented. gdml.py has gdml_transform, compose_transforms, apply_transform. 14 tests all passing.

title: Research: VD wire connectivity, head/tail convention, and segment rules
description: Research the VD-specific wire geometry conventions by examining protodunevd GDML files and existing VD wires files (from wire-cell-data or dunevd.py): (1) How are pairs of U wires connected across a pair of faces, etc for V (W are not connected).  (2) What is the nearness criterion for pairing wires across faces - 'same X, small gap in Y-Z along wire direction': what specific tolerance in cm? (3) What is the head/tail convention for VD wires - which end points toward the channel electronics? Is it related to which face is 'top' vs 'bottom' in the GDML? (4) How are segment numbers assigned within a connected pair? Produce written design notes via 'bd update --design=...' with enough specificity to implement T5.3. After completing this, create new beads tasks for the VD connectivity implementation.
design:
VD wire connectivity conventions (from analysis of protodunevd-wires-larsoft-v3.json.bz2 and dunevd.py):

PLANES THAT ARE CROSS-FACE CONNECTED:
U (ident=0) and V (ident=1) induction planes only. W (ident=2, collection) wires are NEVER connected across faces; all W wires have segment=0 only. For anode 0 in the reference JSON: 97 cross-face channels per U and V plane out of ~287 wires per face per plane.

FACE BOUNDARY AND PAIRING CRITERION:
The two faces of a VD anode (open-book: side-by-side in Y, coplanar in X drift) meet at a shared boundary plane. At this boundary, the endpoint of a wire segment from face A exactly coincides in world-frame coordinates with one endpoint of the connecting wire segment from face B (same X, same Y, same Z to floating-point precision in the JSON). 
Implementation rule: two wire segments (one from each face of the same anode) are connected if they share an endpoint within ε = 1 mm in world frame. This is well below the wire pitch (4.76 mm). The boundary Y-position is implicitly defined by the TPC volume extents.
Geometric detail: the two faces have OPPOSITE Z-components of their wire direction due to rPlus180AboutY rotation of the Bot TPC. U wires in face0 (Top, identity rotation) run at +60 deg from Y toward +Z; U wires in face1 (Bot, rPlus180AboutY) run at +60 deg from Y toward -Z. They meet in a V-shape at the face boundary.

HEAD/TAIL CONVENTION FOR VD:
head = endpoint at higher Y_world (physically upward in GDML world frame). This is consistent with dunevd.py comment 'always point upward in Y'. In the reference JSON all wire segments (both seg=0 and seg=1 of cross-face wires, and standalone wires) have head.y > tail.y. For GDML-based extraction: after computing world-frame endpoints from the full transform chain, set head = endpoint with higher Y_GDML.

SEGMENT NUMBER ASSIGNMENT:
- Standalone wire (on one face only): segment=0.
- Cross-face connected wire pair: assign segment=0 to the segment on the face with HIGHER face.ident (= face1, Bot TPC, lower Y range); assign segment=1 to the segment on face with LOWER face.ident (= face0, Top TPC, higher Y range). Rule: seg = 1 - face.ident for ident in {0,1}.
- The lengths of seg=0 and seg=1 can vary widely (seg=0 can be shorter or longer than seg=1 depending on wire position). The assignment is purely face-ident-based, not length-based.
- Both seg=0 and seg=1 point head-upward (+Y) independently.

IMPLEMENTATION NOTE FOR wcpy-nqh:
After extracting world-frame wire endpoints from GDML (one set per TPC/face), group faces into anode pairs. For each anode's U and V planes, run an O(N) spatial matching: build a dict keyed by (round(x,0), round(y,0), round(z,0)) mm from all endpoints, then for each wire's endpoints look up matches in the other face's endpoint dict. Match threshold: < 1 mm. Channel numbering: the face-1 (Bot) wire's segment gets channel N; the face-0 stub shares channel N. W planes: skip cross-face matching entirely.
close_reason: Research complete. Design notes written to issue. Two follow-up implementation tasks created: wcpy-bs5 (endpoint-matching) and wcpy-r38 (channel/segment assignment). Both block wcpy-nqh.

title: run_one passes rec_only to every app's Dataset, but only xvunet accepts it
description:
wirecell/dnn/__main__.py:680 calls app.Dataset(files, config=..., rec_only=rec_only) unconditionally, but only xvunet's Dataset grew the keyword in e17e426 ("TBD other models (sorry)"). The other four apps raise:

    TypeError: Dataset.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'rec_only'

so run_one is unusable for dnnroi, dnnroi_custom, dnnroi_regres and uvitrio -- including with the flag left at its default, since rec_only is always passed rather than only when true.

Reproduced on this machine:
    uv run wcpy dnn run_one -a dnnroi_custom -c wirecell/dnn/cfg/spng_campaign/jcal-dnnroi-spng-dense_input-mpfile-uplane-pdhd.cfg -l training_results-uplane.pt -n 0 -d gpu <files>
The model builds and its weights load fine; the failure is purely in the dataset construction.

Signatures today:
  dnnroi_custom/data.py:78  Dataset(paths, threshold=0.5, cache=False, config=None)
  xvunet/data.py            accepts rec_only

Found while working wcpy-1so, which reworked the model/checkpoint half of run_one; this is the remaining half and is independent of it.
design: Two options. (a) Add rec_only to the other four Datasets, honouring it where a rec-only read is meaningful and raising a clear error where it is not. (b) Have run_one pass it only when set, so the default path keeps working everywhere and only an explicit --rec-only hits an unsupporting app -- cheaper, and it fails with a message about the app rather than a TypeError. (b) then (a) incrementally is probably right.
acceptance_criteria: run_one works for all five apps without --rec-only; with --rec-only it either works or fails with a message naming the app and the unsupported flag, not a TypeError.

title: Delegate checkpoint-resume resolution to the model classes
description:
Resuming a run is becoming architecture-dependent, and the generic harness in
wirecell/dnn/__main__.py currently has to know model-specific facts to do it correctly. Move
the resolution and validation onto the Network classes, keeping the loading mechanics generic.

## What is wrong today

Order of operations in train() is: build Network from [model] (:135), build Optimizer from the
model's parameters (:137), then if --load, io.load_checkpoint overwrites both (:153).

1. REDUNDANT AND SILENT. With --load given, XViewUNet.__init__ still loads all three
   unet_checkpoints (~40M params, three file reads) and then init_checkpoint, and --load
   overwrites the whole model state afterwards. The cfg loads are pure waste and --load wins
   with no warning, so a user who believes their unet_checkpoints are in effect is simply
   wrong. Under DDP the wasted I/O is paid per rank.

2. THE OPTIMIZER'S PARAMETER SET IS FIXED BY THE CONFIG, NOT THE CHECKPOINT. xvunet's Optimizer
   filters on p.requires_grad, and freeze_unets is applied in __init__ before the optimizer is
   built. Measured on a small model: 52 optimizer tensors when frozen vs 274 unfrozen. So the
   training regime is decided by the cfg while the state being restored came from elsewhere.

   Note freezing itself DOES survive --load -- requires_grad_(False) is set before the
   optimizer exists and load_state_dict only copies values. Verified: trunk params with
   requires_grad=True is 0 after loading into a frozen build. The problem is not that the model
   silently unfreezes; it is that a regime mismatch surfaces as:

     ValueError: loaded state dict contains a parameter group that doesn't match the size of
     optimizer's group

   which is loud but says nothing about freeze_unets, the actual cause.

3. model_args IS STORED FLAT. __main__.py:203 does **model_args inside the this_run dict, so
   view_splits, d_model, attn_mode land as siblings of ntrain, batch, device, name. A resolver
   cannot tell model config from run metadata, and because **model_args comes last a colliding
   key silently wins -- 'name' being the plausible one.

## Proposed design

Delegate RESOLUTION AND VALIDATION to the model; keep MECHANICS (io.load_checkpoint, the
Optimizer factory) generic. The model-specific knowledge is which keys mean what, not how to
call load_state_dict.

On Network, two declarations and one classmethod:

    INIT_KEYS = ('unet_checkpoints', 'init_checkpoint')
        cfg keys that only seed a fresh run.  A full checkpoint overwrites whatever they
        produced, so honouring them on resume is wasted I/O and misleading.

    STRUCTURAL_KEYS = ('view_splits','chunks','d_model','n_heads','n_layers','band',
                       'ffn_mult','n_input_channels','n_classes','freeze_unets')
        cfg keys fixing structure or regime.  A resume must agree with the checkpoint on all
        of these or the restored optimizer state is invalid.

    @classmethod
    def resolve_config(cls, cfg, checkpoint_args=None) -> dict
        Fresh run: cfg unchanged.  Resuming: drop INIT_KEYS with a log line, and check
        STRUCTURAL_KEYS against what the checkpoint recorded, failing here with a clear message
        instead of later as an opaque optimizer param-group error.

Harness side:

    ck = dnn.io.load_checkpoint_raw(load) if load else None
    model_cfg = resolve(app.Network, config.get('model', {}), ck)

where resolve() is a two-line helper using getattr(NetworkCls, 'resolve_config', None) and
falling through to identity. THE OTHER FOUR APPS THEN NEED NO CHANGES, which matters -- they
have already been touched twice recently for the **kwargs migration.

## Also fix

Store model_args nested (model_args=model_args) rather than spread, so
checkpoint['runs'][n]['model_args'] is unambiguous and cannot collide with run metadata.

## Implementation notes

- The checkpoint must be read BEFORE the model is built (to resolve) and again to load state.
  For a 167 MB file that double read is worth avoiding: read once with load_checkpoint_raw and
  add io.load_checkpoint_from(obj, model, optimizer) taking the already-loaded dict.
- Old checkpoints store model_args flat, so a missing 'model_args' key should mean 'unknown,
  skip validation with a warning', not an error. Do not strand existing checkpoints.
- freeze_unets in STRUCTURAL_KEYS is the point of the exercise: it turns today's cryptic
  ValueError into 'checkpoint was trained with freeze_unets=true, config says false -- use
  init_checkpoint to change regime'.
- Keep the stage-1 -> stage-2 path exactly as it is: init_checkpoint loads weights only with a
  fresh optimizer, which is correct. Document it as THE way to change regime, with --load
  reserved for same-regime resume.
acceptance_criteria: --load with unet_checkpoints or init_checkpoint in cfg skips those loads and logs that it did; a freeze_unets mismatch between checkpoint and config fails with a message naming freeze_unets, not an optimizer param-group error; model_args stored nested and retrievable as checkpoint['runs'][n]['model_args']; checkpoints lacking model_args still load, with a warning; the other four apps require no source changes; the checkpoint file is read once, not twice
close_reason:
Resume resolution now lives on the model class.

Network gains INIT_KEYS (dropped on --load, since the checkpoint supersedes what they seed), STRUCTURAL_KEYS (validated; mismatch raises naming the key, with freeze_unets pointing at init_checkpoint) and, added during review, ADVISORY_KEYS = attn_mode -- a mode change loads cleanly so it warns rather than fails, which keeps the wcpy-fta/wcpy-672 ablations possible while killing the silent case. RECORDED_KEYS drives recovery of the model config from pre-nesting checkpoints, where it sat flat among the run metadata, so existing checkpoints are validated rather than merely warned about.

Harness: resolve_model_config() falls through to identity via getattr, so the other four apps needed no source changes; the checkpoint is read once (io.load_checkpoint_from) instead of twice; ValueError is re-raised as click.ClickException so a rejected resume prints as Error: ... rather than a traceback. model_args is stored nested.

run_one had the same defect and was failing outright wherever the cfg's unet_checkpoints had moved -- it honoured them and then overwrote every weight. It now uses the same read-once/resolve/build/load sequence, via a new io.load_model_state_from(), which also lets it accept a bare state dict and strip DDP module. prefixes.

Verified against the real 167 MB training_results_0_1712.pt (the wcpy-pqx diverged run, flat model_args, attn_mode=intra) on an RTX 4090 with bf16, plus CPU: same-regime resume continues as run 1 epoch 6; intra->all warns then trains; freeze_unets true->false is refused by name (previously the opaque param-group ValueError); run_one produces sane output (sigmoid positive fraction 0.97% vs label 1.02%). 59 unit tests pass, 26 of them in test_xvunet.py.

title: Add the ability to diagnose the model run-to-run i.e. extracting key parameters like xvunet gamma-gates
Add Learning Rate Scheduling
description:
Add optional learning-rate scheduling to the dnn training harness.

Motivation: per-epoch gains in the xvunet stage-1 run decayed sharply (17.3 -> 2.1 -> 1.5 ->
0.7 -> 0.5 -> 0.3 pp), which is the profile a decaying schedule usually improves -- a large
early rate to make fast progress, decayed later to settle rather than bounce. Currently the
lr is fixed for a whole run and the only way to change it is to stop, edit the config and
restart with a new --load.

Plumbing is mostly in place: obj_with_config(app.Optimizer, config, 'optimizer', ...) already
passes the [optimizer] section as **kwargs, so scheduler keys can ride in the same section
with no new CLI surface.

Design points to settle:

1. WHERE IT LIVES. Optimizer is per-app (wirecell/dnn/apps/*/__init__.py), but the epoch loop
   that would call scheduler.step() is in wirecell/dnn/__main__.py around line 221, and the
   per-epoch work is in wirecell/dnn/train.py Classifier.epoch/.evaluate. Options: a per-app
   Scheduler factory alongside Optimizer, mirroring the existing pattern; or a single shared
   builder in train.py driven by [optimizer] keys. The per-app route matches the current
   design but duplicates a scheduler across five apps that would likely all want the same one.

2. STEP GRANULARITY. Per-epoch (call after trainer.epoch) is simplest and matches the loop.
   Per-step (inside Classifier.epoch) is needed for warmup, which is the one schedule this
   model might genuinely want -- see note on zero-init gating below. Decide before writing,
   since per-step requires touching train.py and per-epoch does not.

3. CHECKPOINT STATE. dnn.io.save_checkpoint stores model_state_dict and optimizer_state_dict
   plus arbitrary kwds. A scheduler has its own state_dict (last_epoch, and for plateau
   schedulers the tracked best). If it is not saved and reloaded, resuming with --load
   restarts the schedule from step 0 at the original lr, which silently undoes the decay.
   Add scheduler_state_dict to save_checkpoint/load_checkpoint.

4. THE TWO-STAGE BOUNDARY. Stage 2 uses init_checkpoint (weights only, not --load, because
   optimizer param groups differ once trunks unfreeze) and divides the lr by 10 by hand. A
   schedule has to be defined across that boundary: either restart it at stage 2 with the
   lower base lr, or carry it. Restarting is probably right since the param groups change,
   but it should be an explicit decision recorded in the config, not an accident.

5. WARMUP AND THE ZERO-INIT GATES. This model's cross-view branch is gated by zero-init
   LayerScale, so early training is spent opening the gates and the effective gradient scale
   changes a lot over the first epoch. A warmup may interact with that differently than with
   an ordinary network -- worth measuring rather than assuming, and worth keeping the option
   to disable it entirely.

6. LR IS NOT RECORDED PER EPOCH. epoch_history entries hold train/eval losses only. With a
   schedule the lr becomes a per-epoch variable, so it should be recorded there or the loss
   curve is uninterpretable after the fact.

SEQUENCING: this should land AFTER the mode ablation (wcpy-672) or be pinned across it. See
that issue -- a schedule changes what 'converged loss' means and adds a hyperparameter that
can interact with the mode being tested.
acceptance_criteria: Scheduler is optional and off by default, so existing configs are unchanged; configured from the [optimizer] section with no new CLI flags; scheduler state is saved to and restored from checkpoints so --load resumes mid-schedule; per-epoch lr is recorded in epoch_history; step granularity (per-epoch vs per-step) is chosen deliberately and documented; behaviour across the stage-1 to stage-2 boundary is explicit

title: xvunet ablation: evaluate a trained model under restricted attention modes
description:
Take a model trained under one attention mode and evaluate it under the others, to ask which pathways a trained model actually uses. Nearly free: attn_mode is runtime state and never changes parameter shapes, so one checkpoint evaluates under every mode with no retraining. Can be run today against training_results_0_1414.pt.

INTERPRETATION LIMITS -- these bound what the result can support:

1. Mode swaps are NOT decomposable. Masking is applied before softmax, so restricting the key set renormalises the surviving weights. Evaluating an all-trained model under inter is not 'remove the intra contribution', it is a different normalisation over a different key set. intra and inter partition the attention PAIRS exactly, but their outputs do not sum to the all output. Do not report them as additive contributions.

2. Degradation is ambiguous in one direction only. A model evaluated outside its training configuration may degrade because it is brittle, not because the removed pathway carried signal. The safe inference is the negative one: if evaluating under 'none' barely hurts, attention genuinely is not being used. The converse does not follow.

CLEANER COMPANION MEASUREMENT: sweep the gammas from their trained values down to zero instead of switching modes. Because the gates are exactly zero-init, gamma=0 recovers the trunk output bit-exactly, so this interpolates smoothly from the trained model to the baseline without altering attention's normalisation. It yields a contribution curve rather than a single point, and it avoids limit 1 entirely. Both XViewUNet.gammas (per view, output head) and each block's gamma1/gamma2 (LayerScale) can be swept; sweep them separately to separate the fused-correction path from the in-block residual branches.

Baseline for reference on training_results_0_1414.pt: output gammas -0.339, -0.292, +0.473; block LayerScale components up to 0.98, so the gates are well open and the attention path is active.
acceptance_criteria: Trained checkpoint evaluated under all five modes on a fixed eval split; results reported without additive-decomposition language; gamma sweep to zero produces a contribution curve terminating at the frozen-trunk baseline; the 'none barely hurts' negative inference is stated explicitly as the only safe one-directional conclusion

title: xvunet ablation: train each attention mode end to end and compare
description:
Train stage-1 (frozen trunks) once per attention mode and compare converged eval loss, to answer whether cross-view attention helps and which connectivity is best.

Why this comparison is clean: gates are zero-init, so every mode is bit-exact equal to the trunks at step 0, and mode changes connectivity only -- parameter count and initial loss are identical across modes. Differences are attributable to what each mode may attend to.

Modes: legacy, all, intra, inter, none. Include none as the control: it still runs the FFN branch, so none != trunk baseline. That gives a decomposition -- (none vs trunks) is what the extra FFN capacity buys, (all vs none) is what attention buys. Without it, 'attention helps' is confounded with 'more parameters help'.

PROTOCOL (both items below have bitten this project before, see the traps section):
1. Compute the frozen-trunk baseline for each configuration BEFORE any optimizer step, not from the first recorded epoch.
2. Run every mode on the same execution path (all single-process, or all DDP at the same world size).
3. Report loss relative to that configuration's own baseline, not absolute.
4. Multiple seeds per mode. One seed cannot separate a few-percent mode difference from run-to-run noise.
5. Decide equal-epochs or equal-wall-clock in advance. Per-step costs differ a lot: none 151, intra 232, legacy 268, inter 299, all 340 ms. At equal epochs, all gets 2.3x the compute of none.

Cost estimate: stage 1 reached -22.9% in about 15 min on one 4090, so 5 modes x 3 seeds is roughly 4 GPU-hours.

Prediction to record before running: the embedding probe found W face 1 carries essentially no positional structure (dc=0.852) because it receives far less signal than face 0. Modes whose behaviour hinges on W1 should therefore show little, and intra on W1 may be near-meaningless. Committing to this in advance makes the outcome interpretable either way.
acceptance_criteria: Per-configuration frozen-trunk baseline computed pre-training and recorded; all runs on one execution path; >=3 seeds per mode; results reported relative to baseline with seed spread shown; both equal-epoch and equal-wall-clock views reported, or the choice justified; none-mode control included so attention is separated from FFN capacity

title: xvunet: banded attention has no relative-time encoding, cannot distinguish t-s from t+s
description:
BandedAttentionBlock gives a query at tick t access to keys from t-band..t+band, but nothing marks which offset a key came from, so the block cannot represent a time-asymmetric preference.

Mechanism. In BandedAttentionBlock.forward, kb and vb are built by concatenating the rolled copies along the token axis (wirecell/dnn/models/xvunet.py:176-177), so the keys for offset s occupy columns [i*N:(i+1)*N]. No per-offset term is ever added. Because kb and vb are concatenated in the same order, permuting the offset blocks permutes keys and values together, and attention is permutation-equivariant over key positions -- so swapping the s=-1 and s=+1 blocks leaves the output bit-identical. The offset is not merely unencoded, it is structurally invisible.

The model can still react to a key's content, since k[t-1] and k[t+1] generally differ. What it cannot do is learn a positional prior such as 'weight the past more than the future', independent of content.

There is no absolute tick encoding either: pos_embed is shaped (1, d_model, ntok, 1) (xvunet.py:274) so it broadcasts over T and carries channel-chunk identity only.

Whether this matters is an open question worth measuring rather than assuming -- induction-plane responses are bipolar and drift is directional, so a time-asymmetric prior is physically plausible.

Options, cheapest first:
1. A learned per-offset embedding, shape (2*band+1, d_model), added into the corresponding column blocks of kb (and optionally vb) after the rolls.
2. A per-offset scalar added to the attention logits. This shares the float attn_mask path with wcpy-exp, so the two should be designed together.
3. A general relative-time encoding over the band (T5-style learned bias, or RoPE on the time axis).

Option 1 or 2 keeps the zero-init gating intact, so the bit-exact-at-init property and the frozen-trunk baseline survive. Verify that explicitly, since it is what makes the two-stage curriculum valid.

Suggested check before building anything: assert that swapping the outer offset blocks of kb and vb leaves the block output unchanged. That pins the current behaviour and turns into a regression test once a fix lands.
acceptance_criteria: A test pins the current offset-permutation invariance; a per-offset encoding or logit bias is added; bit-exactness at init is re-verified (fresh model still equals the trunks); an A/B against the current frozen-trunk baseline records whether the asymmetry actually helps

title: xvunet: Allow for different attention masking modes in BandedAttentionBlock._band_mask creation
description:
## Context
For ablation studies, would like to test with no attention; only inter-channel attention within a given plane; only inter-plane attention: in other words, a channel from one plane can only see all channels from other planes, not itself; and all-channel attention (the current implementation).
design: Current attention formed by a 'primitive' of t = torch.arange(T). Might be good to abstract this away to a user-defined function that provides this primitive
notes:
IMPLEMENTED AND COMMITTED in 4b6fa36. Performance question investigated and settled: keep
the committed (grouped) implementation. No further work outstanding.

WHAT IS IN 4b6fa36:
- ATTN_MODES = (legacy, all, intra, inter, none) in wirecell/dnn/models/xvunet.py
- BandedAttentionBlock._attend(q,k,v) accepts Nq != Nk; _key_spans(seg) merges allowed spans;
  modes are realised by handing each query segment a restricted key set (grouped approach)
- XViewUNet.token_segments = [(lo,hi,view)]; XViewUNet.set_attention_mode()
- apps/xvunet/model.py: attn_mode config key + passthrough setter
- DEFAULT IS 'all' at both levels. legacy is opt-in via attn_mode=legacy and is the only
  mode that lets the two W faces attend to each other.
- segments/attn_mode are plain attributes, not buffers/params, so state_dict is unchanged
  and one checkpoint evaluates under every mode.

VERIFIED:
- legacy bit-exact vs pre-modes code (vs ad5e5a4, torch.equal True)
- mode reachability matches the rule table for all 5 modes (perturbation test)
- all == legacy bit-exact when no view has 2 segments; forbidden set is exactly the two
  W0xW1 blocks, 7200 token pairs
- backward works under all modes with activation checkpointing; grads finite
- GPU bf16 autocast at production geometry: all modes finite
- 47 tests pass; real checkpoint training_results_0_1414.pt loads and runs

ALSO FIXED: test_banded_locality was passing with attention switched off (uniform +1.0
perturbation is removed exactly by LayerNorm as the token mean, so neighbour ticks moved
by ~1e-7 of float rounding, not attention; and only containment was asserted). Now uses a
non-uniform perturbation, a tolerance, and an equality assertion.

CORRECTED PERFORMANCE NUMBERS -- an earlier revision of these notes had this wrong.
Median of 5 interleaved reps x 3 steps, RTX 4090, bf16 autocast, production geometry,
B=1, frozen trunks, use_checkpoint=True:

  mode     ms/step   peak GiB
  legacy     268.2       3.53
  all        340.1       5.13     <- default, 1.27x legacy
  intra      231.9       3.76     <- FASTER than legacy
  inter      299.2       4.61
  none       150.7       2.45

METHODOLOGY WARNING: the FIRST timed repetition runs ~25% fast and then settles (198 ms
vs 268 ms for byte-identical code). Every number in the earlier revision of these notes
came from a single unrepeated measurement and was wrong. Always warm up, repeat, and take
medians. Also check nvidia-smi first: GPU 0 was being used by another user during part of
this work, which caused a spurious OOM.

Two claims from the earlier notes that were WRONG and are retracted:
- 'restricting the key set buys nothing' -- false, intra at 232 ms beats legacy at 268
- 'all is 1.5x slower than legacy' -- it is 1.27x, and that is inherent to forbidding
  pairs, not a fixable inefficiency

ALTERNATIVE TRIED AND REJECTED (fix b, static view mask): roll once, one SDPA call per
tick range, forbid pairs with a static (N,M) view mask broadcast over batch and tick, with
the interior ticks split from the 2*band edge ticks that need the wraparound mask. It works
and is correct, but measured SLOWER in every restricted mode: all 363 vs 340, intra 322 vs
232, inter 347 vs 299. Its only advantage is memory: all 3.97 vs 5.13 GiB, inter 3.96 vs
4.61. Revisit only if memory becomes the binding constraint rather than time.
Two implementation traps found while building it, worth knowing if it is ever retried:
- SDPA must get 4-D inputs. A 5-D (B,T,h,L,dh) layout drops it onto the math path, which
  materialises the whole (B,T,h,N,M) weight matrix and OOMs at production size. Slice ticks
  before folding them into the batch axis, never after.
- legacy must keep the original single-call formulation. Passing attn_mask=None on the
  interior lets SDPA take a different (flash) kernel, which costs bit-exactness (~3e-8).

NOT VERIFIED: DDP; views with 3+ segments; inter with a single view (empty key set branch);
torchscript trace with the new mode branching (a trace bakes in the active mode).

CORRECTION (appended after close): the claim above that the static view-mask alternative is
inherently more expensive is WRONG. Isolated measurement of the mask alone -- same single SDPA
call, production shapes (B*T=1500, h=4, N=320, M=960, dh=24), bf16, fwd+bwd, median of 7 reps
x 5 iters after warmup:

  attn_mask                  median ms   mask MiB
  None (no mask)                  0.12       0.00
  (1,1,1,M)   query-constant      0.18       0.00
  (B*T,1,1,M) = legacy            0.22       1.37
  (N,M)       query-varying       0.23       0.29
  (1,1,N,M)   query-varying       0.23       0.29

A query-varying mask costs the SAME as legacy's current one (0.23 vs 0.22 ms, inside the
run-to-run spread) and is 4.7x SMALLER (0.29 vs 1.37 MiB); peak memory identical. The mask
shape is free. The slowdown attributed to it came entirely from what was wrapped around it:
the three-way tick split, the slicing of q/kb/vb, and the final cat.

Re-reading the mode numbers in that light:
- intra grouped 232 vs masked 322 is NOT a mask effect. Grouped does 1/4 the attention work
  (81,600 logit pairs vs 307,200) because a restricted key set means fewer logits; masked
  always computes the full NxM and discards part of it.
- all grouped 340 vs masked 363 is the split overhead, about 7%.

IF THE MASKED DESIGN IS EVER REVISITED, prefer this shape over the three-way split: run ONE
full-T SDPA with the (N,M) view mask -- correct on the interior, wrong on the 2*band edge
ticks -- then a second tiny SDPA over just those edge ticks with the combined mask
((B*2b,1,N,M), about 0.6 MiB), and splice out of place. Total mask memory stays under 1 MiB
regardless of T or B, and the big call consumes contiguous tensors so its reshape is free --
which matters at B>1, where slicing the interior forces a copy of kb/vb (3x the token width).
Caveat: the big call's edge output is invalid but FINITE, so nothing fails loudly if the
fixup is forgotten. Pin it with a test.

Rejected alternative: caching a combined (T,1,N,M) mask. One call, simplest control flow, but
440 MiB as bool at T=1500/N=320/M=960, 879 MiB if SDPA converts it to a bf16 bias, 1.72 GiB
if fp32; linear in T; and it cannot broadcast to a B*T fold for B>1 without materialising B
copies (keeping B separate needs 5-D inputs, which drop SDPA onto the math path and OOM). It
spends exactly the memory the masked design exists to save.

DECISION UNCHANGED: keep the committed grouped implementation. Masked is roughly neutral on
the default mode, worse on intra, and its memory win addresses a constraint this project does
not have (peak 5.13 GiB on 24 GiB cards; notes record ms/sample flat in batch size). Revisit
if memory becomes binding, or when wcpy-0mj is implemented -- that needs a per-offset float
term in this same mask path, so redesigning then amortises the re-verification.
close_reason: Implemented and committed in 4b6fa36: runtime-selectable attention scopes (legacy/all/intra/inter/none) via per-query-segment key restriction, default 'all' so the two W faces never attend to each other. Verified: legacy bit-exact vs pre-modes code, mode reachability matches the rule table, backward works under bf16 autocast with checkpointing, 47 tests pass. Performance question settled -- kept the grouped implementation; a static view-mask alternative measured slower in every restricted mode and was reverted. Corrected timings and a methodology warning about unrepeated measurements are in the notes.

title: xvunet: try a feature-space residual instead of a logit-space one
description:
The cross-view correction is currently added in LOGIT space
(wirecell/dnn/models/xvunet.py:543-544):

    logits = trunks[iv].segmap(feats[iseg]) + gammas[iv] * heads[iv](fused)

where fused = fuses[iv](cat(feats, up)) and heads[iv] is a fresh 1x1 conv, Conv2d(feat,
n_classes, 1) at :373, initialised randomly and independent of the trunk's pretrained segmap.

The alternative is to add the correction in FEATURE space and let the pretrained segmap
produce the logits:

    logits = trunks[iv].segmap(feats[iseg] + gammas[iv] * refine(fused))

with refine a Conv2d(feat, feat, 1) replacing heads. The gating and the bit-exact-at-init
property are unchanged: gamma=0 still reproduces the trunk output exactly, so warm-starting,
the frozen-trunk baseline and the two-stage curriculum all still hold.

WHY IT MIGHT BE BETTER
- It reuses the pretrained segmap rather than training a second output layer from scratch.
  The correction inherits the trunk head's calibration instead of having to relearn it.
- The correction is constrained to be expressible as a perturbation of trunk features, which
  is a stronger inductive bias and closer to what the rest of this design assumes.
- It is what Non-local Neural Networks does (Wang, Girshick, Gupta, He, CVPR 2018,
  arXiv:1711.07971): attention inserted as a residual in feature space, z = W_z(y) + x, with
  W_z zero-initialised precisely so the block can be dropped into a pretrained network without
  disturbing it. That is the same argument the gammas make here, so matching its placement is
  consistent.

WHY IT MIGHT BE WORSE
- Less freedom. A logit-space head can express corrections that no feature perturbation can,
  since segmap is a fixed linear map and its null space is unreachable from feature space.
- In stage 1 the trunks are frozen, so segmap is frozen too. The correction must then push
  features through a fixed linear map, which may be a real constraint early on. Worth checking
  whether it matters more in stage 1 (frozen) than stage 2 (unfrozen).

SCOPE: small. Replace heads[iv] with refine, move the addition inside segmap at :543-544, and
keep fuses unchanged. Parameter count changes from Conv2d(feat, n_classes, 1) to
Conv2d(feat, feat, 1), i.e. from feat*n_classes to feat*feat -- with feat=32, n_classes=1
that is 32 -> 1024 per view, still negligible against 40.5M.

BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY: this changes state_dict keys (heads -> refine) and shapes, so existing
xvunet checkpoints will not load into the new variant and vice versa. Make it a config flag
(e.g. residual_space = logit | feature, default logit) rather than a replacement, so the two
can be compared and old checkpoints keep working.

MEASURE IT AS AN ABLATION, not a swap: same protocol as wcpy-672 -- fixed ddp-split-seed,
several runs without --manual-seed for a distribution, and a per-configuration frozen-trunk
baseline computed before the first optimizer step.
acceptance_criteria: residual_space is a config option defaulting to the current logit-space behaviour; feature-space variant is bit-exact equal to the trunks at init (gamma=0), verified by the existing zero-init test; existing checkpoints still load under the default; both variants compared under the wcpy-672 protocol with a shared split and multiple seeds

title: Implement HD channel assignment (assign_hd_channels)
description:
Implement HD wire connectivity and channel assignment for the closed-book geometry.

**What needs to be done:**
Implement assign_hd_channels() in wirecell/util/gdml.py that assigns channel IDs and segment numbers to wires from a pair of HD anode faces.

**Algorithm (from wcpy-6dd design notes):**
1. W/Z plane (ident=2): assign unique channels sequentially, segment=0, no cross-face sharing.
2. U and V planes (ident=0,1): use Z-boundary rank matching:
   a. Find Z_min and Z_max of the active volume (min/max Z of all wire endpoints in the face)
   b. At each Z boundary, collect wire endpoints from face0 and face1 within ~1mm in Z
   c. Sort face0 endpoints by Y descending, sort face1 endpoints by Y descending
   d. Match by rank: face0[i] and face1[i] are the same physical wire
   e. The primary face (seg=0) is the one whose head is at the highest Y (closer to electronics)
   f. Subsequent segments are numbered 1, 2 in order away from electronics
3. Assign globally unique channel IDs: offset by anode_idx * channels_per_anode

**Expected results (from reference file protodunehd-wires-larsoft-v1.json.bz2):**
- 2560 unique channels per anode (800 U + 800 V + 480 W per face × 2 faces, with sharing)
- U/V: 400 wires have 2 segments, 348 have 3 segments per plane pair
- Head always points in +Y direction

- role_patterns: face=volTPC(Inner|Outer), plane=volTPCPlane[UVZ](Inner|Outer), wire=volTPCWire(([UV]\d+|Vert)(Inner|Outer)), detector=volCryostat
- connectivity_mode: hd
- pair_mode: yz_centroid (HD: same YZ centroid, opposite X = one anode)

design:
HD connectivity design notes (from reference wires analysis):

DETECTOR STRUCTURE
- 4 anodes, 8 faces (2 per anode), 24 planes (3 per face)
- 2560 unique channels per anode: U=800, V=800, W=480 (per-face, no sharing)
- Channels sequential across anodes: anode 0 = [0..2559], anode 1 = [2560..5119], etc.

WHICH PLANES WRAP
- U (ident=0): YES, up to 3 segments
- V (ident=1): YES, up to 3 segments
- W/Z (ident=2): NO, segment=0 only (collection plane, 480 wires per face, no cross-face sharing)

SEGMENT STRUCTURE (U plane, anode 0, 800 channels, 1148 wires per face)
- ch 0..347 (348): 3 segments - face1-seg0, face0-seg1, face1-seg2 (primary = face1)
- ch 348..399 (52): 2 segments - face1-seg0, face0-seg1 (primary = face1)
- ch 400..747 (348): 3 segments - face0-seg0, face1-seg1, face0-seg2 (primary = face0)
- ch 748..799 (52): 2 segments - face0-seg0, face1-seg1 (primary = face0)
- seg=0: the segment ending at electronics (head = electronics = +Y direction)
- seg=1: first continuation after wrapping at a Z boundary
- seg=2: second continuation (wraps again at other Z boundary back to primary face)

HEAD/TAIL CONVENTION
- Head points in +Y direction for BOTH face0 and face1 wires (confirmed)
- Consistent across all plane types

WRAP GEOMETRY (critical - different from VD)
- Wires wrap at the Z boundaries (Z_min and Z_max of active volume), NOT at Y boundaries
- At the wrap point: face0 and face1 endpoints have EXACTLY the same Z coordinate
- But Y coordinates differ by a constant gap of ~9.4mm (the cathode gap between the TPC volumes)
- Adjacent wires have Y spacing of ~8mm at the Z boundary

WHY 3D ENDPOINT PROXIMITY FAILS FOR HD
- Faces are ~106mm apart in X (the drift distance) => 3D distance is ~106mm even for matching wires
- Y gap at wrap points = 9.4mm > wire pitch in Y = 8mm => even YZ proximity has ambiguity
- Cannot safely use the VD endpoint-proximity algorithm for HD

CORRECT MATCHING ALGORITHM: Z-BOUNDARY RANK MATCHING
At each Z boundary (Z_min and Z_max):
1. Find all wire endpoints in face0 with Z coord within ~1mm of Z_boundary
2. Find all wire endpoints in face1 with Z coord within ~1mm of Z_boundary
3. Sort face0 endpoints by Y (descending = toward electronics)
4. Sort face1 endpoints by Y (descending)
5. Match face0[i] with face1[i] by rank - these are the same physical wire
Rationale: face0 and face1 endpoints at each boundary are offset by a constant Y gap, so rank ordering is preserved and safe even though gap < pitch.

GDML VOLUME NAMING (protodunehd_v8_refactored.gdml)
- Faces: volTPCInner, volTPCOuter
- Planes: volTPCPlane{U,V,Z}{Inner,Outer}
- Wires: volTPCWire{U,V}{N}{Inner,Outer} (N=number), collection: volTPCWireVert{Inner,Outer}
- Detector: volCryostat
- Role patterns:
    face:     r'volTPC(Inner|Outer)'
    plane:    r'volTPCPlane[UVZ](Inner|Outer)'
    wire:     r'volTPCWire(([UV]\d+|Vert)(Inner|Outer))'
    detector: r'volCryostat'

ANODE PAIRING
- 8 TPC placements in cryostat: 4 Inner and 4 Outer, alternating pattern
- Each Inner/Outer pair at same Z column = one anode
- HD closed-book: group by Y-Z centroid (same centroid = same anode)
- Unlike VD (side-by-side Y), HD faces have same Y-Z but opposite X drift direction

Key architectural decisions for gdml-to-wires (from planning session):
1. COORDINATES: wire endpoints must be in GDML world frame (full transform chain required).
2. FACE-TO-ANODE PAIRING: VD = 'open book' (two faces co-planar, side-by-side, same X/drift coordinate); HD = 'closed book' (two faces parallel and opposite, same Y-Z extents but opposite X).

5. HEAD/TAIL: head = toward electronics. HD top sub-detector: generally upward (+Y). HD bottom: generally downward (-Y). VD: needs research (wcpy-zv1).

GDML rotation convention (confirmed by research, wcpy-8o7): <rotation x=a y=b z=c unit=deg/> stores a PASSIVE rotation M = Mz(c)*My(b)*Mx(a) (extrinsic XYZ order). The ACTIVE local-to-world rotation is M^{-1} = M^T. In code: R = Rotation.from_euler('xyz', [a,b,c], degrees=True).inv().as_matrix() — use lowercase 'xyz' (extrinsic), the .inv() is MANDATORY. GDML tube z attribute = FULL length; half_L = z_gdml/2. Wire axis is local Z; endpoints: tail=[0,0,-half_L], head=[0,0,+half_L]. Composition: T_world = T_cryo @ T_tpc @ T_plane @ T_wire (parent first, child last).

Wire-Cell wires schema summary (wirecell/util/wires/schema.py):
Hierarchy (trunk to leaf): Store -> Detector -> Anode -> Face -> Plane -> Wire -> Point.
Children are referenced by INDEX into flat arrays: Store holds flat lists of each type.
- Point(x, y, z): world-frame coordinates in WCT units (mm base unit)
- Wire(ident, channel, segment, tail, head): tail/head are Point indices. head = toward electronics.
- Plane(ident, wires): wires = list of Wire indices in INCREASING PITCH order. ident = 0/1/2 for U/V/W.
- Face(ident, planes): planes list in U/V/W order.
- Anode(ident, faces): faces list.
- Detector(ident, anodes): anodes list.
- Store(detectors, anodes, faces, planes, wires, points): all flat lists.
Persist: wirecell/util/wires/persist.py — load(name) and dump(filename, store) handle .json and .json.bz2.
